 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Approve the single source purchase of meter testing & diagnostic equipment from Radian Research. 

 For information, please contact: Tony Guillen, General Manager- Electric & Gas Utility, 850- 891-5534 or Greg Ozbun, Assistant General Manager - System, 850-891-3030 

 Statement of Issue 

 The City of Tallahassee Electric & Gas Utility continuously seeks to be a leader in the delivery of public service by implementing industry best practices that ensure system reliability. Currently, the City provides electric and gas service to approximately 125,000 customers with 26 different meter styles and configurations. New and replacement meters are bought with future planning in mind and may sit in storage before being installed. While awaiting deployment, vendors often release software and firmware updates that these meters do not receive because they are not in an energized and load controlled state. This item seeks a single source contract for a warmup load board and meter farm that will allow for meters to be updated and retested as they await deployment. Radian Research is the sole vendor that provides equipment compatible with the City’s utility software application. This contract will significantly improve the speed that meters can be replaced and ensure greater system reliability. 

 Recommended Action 

 Option 1: Approve the single source purchase of meter testing and diagnostic equipment from Radian Research. 

 Fiscal Impact 

 The Radian Research Electric Meter Farm and WECO 9200 Warm-Up Load Board total $373,390 and will be purchased from the Electric RR&I fund. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 

 Currently, the City provides electric and gas service to approximately 125,000 customers with 26 different meter styles and configurations. New and replacement meters are bought with future planning in mind and may sit in storage before being installed. While awaiting deployment, vendors often release software and firmware updates that these meters do not receive because they are not in an energized and load controlled state. When these meters are then installed, it can result in Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) network communication issues that impede the collection and transmittal of detailed energy usage data to electric utilities. When this occurs, meters must then be retested to ensure all software/firmware updates are installed prior to redeployment. 

 Given the potential for resource strain considering lead times for acquiring new electric meters is one year, staff recommend purchasing an electric meter farm and Warm-Up Load Board. This will allow the utility to test meters for accuracy, functionality, and compatibility with our AMI systems to significantly improve the speed that meters can be replaced and ensure greater system reliability. Radian Research Inc. is the only vendor that supplies a warm-up load board and meter farm compatible with the utility software application. 

 Department(s) Review 

 Procurement, Resource Management 

 Options 

 1. Approve the single source purchase of meter testing and diagnostic equipment from Radian Research. 

 Pros: The City of Tallahassee would have the meter testing environment needed to validate updates pushed out by the vendor on to our system. 

 Cons: None 

 2. Do not approve the single source award. 

 Pros: Fiscal monies allocated for this equipment could potentially be otherwise allocated for other Electric & Gas use. 

 Cons: The City of Tallahassee would not have the meter testing environment needed to validate updates pushed out by the vendor on to our system. 

 Attachments/References 

 1. Purchase Order and Single Source Justification

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Authorize staff to purchase gas modules, regulators, mounting kits, and other gas accessories from DevTech. 

 For more information, please contact: Stephen Mayfield, Electric and Gas Utility (850) 891-5118. 

 Statement of Issue 
 The Gas Utility has faced difficulty in acquiring gas modules and mounting kits due to supply chain issues. Devtech, an authorized Honeywell Distributor can supply the modules and mounting kits so that service to customers will not be delayed. 

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Authorize staff to purchase gas modules, regulators, mounting kits, and other gas meter accessories from Devtech. 

 Fiscal Impact 
 The expenditure of $1.5 million is within the Electric & Gas Utility warehouse Fund. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 

 Due to supply chain issues, the Electric & Gas Utility has faced difficulty acquiring residential and small commercial gas modules and mounting kits for gas meters. The utility must use Honeywell gas modules for compatibility with our gas equipment, which limits potential vendors' options. 

 Devtech is the sole provider of these products in Florida, and purchasing other products would not be compatible with the City’s system. Devtech is approved as a single source vendor through June 2025, however, City Commission approval is required due to the total expenditure requested. The items purchased include the following:  

 1. Natural Gas Meter Modules: electronic devices that can be added to traditional gas meters to enhance their functionality. These enable remote reading of consumption and integration into the City’s smart grid system.   

 2. Mounting Kits: used to securely install gas meters onto various surfaces, such as walls, poles, or meter bases. They typically include components like brackets, screws, and anchors. The specific type of mounting kit depends on the meter size, installation location, and local regulations. 

 3. Regulators: reduces the high-pressure gas from the main supply line to a safe, low-pressure suitable for household appliances.  

 Options 
 1. Authorize staff to purchase gas modules, regulators, mounting kits, and other gas meter accessories from Devtech. 

 Pros: The Gas Utility will be able to provide residential and small commercial gas service to customers without impacting customer service standards. 

 Cons: Unknown 

 2. Reject the request to purchase Honeywell gas modules, regulators, mounting kits, and other gas meter accessories from Devtech. 

 Pros: None 

 Cons: The Gas Utility will not be able to provide residential and small commercial gas service to customers.

 Fiscal Impact

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 
 This item provides for the first and only public hearing of Ordinance No. 24-O-33 (Attachment #1) to adopt the small-scale map amendment TMA 2024 013 (1932 Miccosukee Road). The adoption of Ordinance No. 24-O-33 would adopt the following amendment to the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan pursuant to Section 163.3187, Florida Statutes. 

 Name: TMA 2024 013 – Miccosukee Road 
 Applicant: Fontana Investments of Tallahassee, Inc. 

 Synopsis : The request is to amend the Future Land Use Map (FLUM) designation from Residential Preservation (RP) to Suburban (SUB) on approximately 0.93 acres (parcel ID 11-20-50-000-0250). The subject property is located on Miccosukee Road between Coombs Drive on the west and Kuhl acres Drive on the east. The subject site is a parcel that has an existing office use on it. The proposal is intended to recognize the existing use, to remove a split land use and zoning, and to remove obsolete Limited Use Site Plans. 

 The amendment is requested from a private entity, Fontana Investments of Tallahassee, Inc., to have the existing office use to remain and to allow a veterinary office to be located on the parcel. The parking lot for the existing office structure is located in the Residential Preservation portion of the property, and the office structure is located in the Suburban portion of the property. Because a change of use is required for the intended veterinary office, it is considered more intense than the current office use. A change of use on the property triggers parking standard requirements, and as a result, the required parking for the site cannot be located in the portion of the property that does not allow the desired use. The proposed amendment and rezoning would resolve this development issue. 

 The amendment would unify the future land use category for a single parcel that is currently split by the Suburban and Residential Preservation categories. The zoning, which is currently split by Office Residential-2 and Residential Preservation-2, would also be unified. This future land use map amendment and concurrent rezoning is only for the portion of the property that is in the Residential Preservation category. The allowable residential density would increase from 6 dwelling units per acre to 16 units per acre and 20,000 square feet of non-residential per acre for office. 

 The site is within the Urban Services Area and infrastructure is available to support the increased allowable density. 

 Based on staff analysis, the subject property does not fully align with the intent of the Residential Preservation FLUM district because of its current use, location and access along the arterial, and because the buildings and uses adjacent east and south are not homogenous, solely residential uses. Additionally, it is adjacent to existing OR-2 zoning which would provide some continuity of use and facilitate the ability to provide and support infill development including a variety of housing types and community facilities. 

 Small-Scale Map Amendment : This is a request to change the Future Land Use Map (FLUM) designation from Residential Preservation (RP) to Suburban (SUB) on approximately 0.93 acres at 1932 Miccosukee Road, fronting Miccosukee Road. This change would allow a veterinary office contemplated by the applicant and resolve development issues created by the split land use and zoning, and the obsolete Limited Use Site Plans. 

 Residential Preservation (RP) (Current) The Residential Preservation category is characterized by single-use, non-commercial residential areas which are predominantly accessed by local streets. The primary function is to protect existing residential areas from incompatible land use intensities and density intrusions. Future development will primarily consist of infill due to the built-out nature of existing residential neighborhoods. Single family, two-family, townhouse, and cluster housing may be permitted within a range of up to 6 units per acre. Consistency with surrounding residential type and density shall be a major determinant in granting development approval. 

 Suburban (Proposed) The proposed Suburban category allows a mixture of office and commercial uses with residential densities up to 20 units per acre. The Suburban land use category is intended to create an environment for economic investment or redevelopment through the mutually advantageous placement of employment and shopping opportunities with convenient access to low to medium density residential land uses. The intent of this district is to provide convenient goods and services to residential areas and employment areas. 

 Concurrent Rezoning: A rezoning application is being processed concurrently with this amendment. A zoning change from Residential Preservation - 2 (RP-2) to Office Residential – 2 (OR-2) will implement the proposed amendment to the Future Land Use Map (FLUM). This is consistent with surrounding land uses and zoning. The rezoning would be quasi-judicial in nature; therefore, any ex parte communications shall be disclosed prior to the item being heard. 

 Consistency with the Comprehensive Plan 
 The proposed amendment is consistent with the following goals, objectives, and policies of the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan: 

 Policy 2.1.6 [L]: Criteria shall be established within local development regulations which require within residential developments the provision of non-residential land uses such as parks, school sites and potential walk-to minor commercial and office opportunities. 

 The residential land use objective of the comprehensive plan seeks to ensure that neighborhoods are protected from density and intensity intrusions while also creating areas that promote walkability by being well-connected to minor commercial and office opportunities. 

 Policy 2.2.5 [L] indicates that employment opportunities should be located near residential areas, and the Suburban category is most suitable for areas outside of the Central Core. The most prevalent development pattern will be a compatibly integrated mix of single-use developments that include low-to-medium density residential, office, and commercial. 

 The subject property is a potential employment location outside of the Central Core that has been operating as an office for many years. The current development pattern represents a compatible integrated mix of low-to-medium density residential and office land uses. The proposed zoning district implements the medium density office residential land use pattern of the future land use map category. This land use pattern reflects the existing uses and serves as a transition to nearby medium and low-density residential uses. 

 Public Comment 

 The Planning Department received three general inquiries for more information about the application. In addition to these three inquiries, comments were received prior to the Local Planning Agency meeting from three residents in opposition to the application. The comments were concerned with the potential for additional traffic that could be generated as a result of increased development at the corner of Miccosukee Road and Kuhlacres Drive. The comments are included in the attached staff report (Attachment #2). 

 Summary of TMA2024 013: 
 Local Planning Agency recommendation on proposed amendment: Approve . 
 Staff analysis on proposed amendment and concurrent rezoning: Consistent . 
 The staff report for this map amendment is included as Attachment #2. 

 Options 
 1. Adopt Ordinance No. 24-O-33, thereby adopting small-scale map amendment TMA2024 013 (1932 Miccosukee Road) to the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan. 

 2. Do not adopt Ordinance 24-O-33, thereby not adopting small-scale map amendment TMA2024 013 (1932 Miccosukee Road) to the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan.

The applicant states that they seek this amendment to provide a unified land use and zoning category for the property. Currently, the parcel is split with a Residential Preservation -2 and Office-Residential – 2 zoning districts as well as a split land use between Residential Preservation and Suburban. 

 The parking lot for the existing office structure is located in the Residential Preservation portion of the property, and the office structure is located in the Suburban portion of the property. The applicant states that the desired use of the existing structure is a veterinarian office, which is a change of use that is considered more intense than the current office use. A change of use on the property triggers parking standard requirements, and as a result, the required parking for the site cannot be located in the portion of the property that does not allow the desired use. 

 The subject property is covered by two Limited Use Site Plans (LUSPs). The first LUSP was enacted in 1984 through Ordinance 84-O-2382. This ordinance rezoned lot 26 from RM-2 (Single and Multiple Residence) to Office-Residential. The second LUSP was enacted in March of 1990 through Ordinance 90-Z-0025AA. This ordinance rezoned lot 25 from A-2 (Agriculture) to RM-1. When the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan was adopted in July of 1990, lots 16 and 26 were covered under the Suburban future land use category that allows Office Residential zoning, and lot 25 became the residential-only category of Residential Preservation. If approved, the accompanying rezoning will rescind the LUSPs. 

 The effect of the rezoning (accompanying the proposed land use change TMA 2024 013) would be to recognize the existing office use, to resolve the split zoning across the parcel, and to remove obsolete Limited Use Site Plans (LUSPs). Details of the proposed change are found in the attached Staff Report, (Attachment #2). 

 Adjacent Existing Uses and Site Analysis 

 The use of the property has most recently been as a publishing office. The parcels directly adjacent to the northern boundary of the property are single family detached homes and are homestead exempted, which indicates that they are owner-occupied residences. The property along Miccosukee Road to the west of Coombs Drive is also classified as an office use, and the Leon County Property Appraiser shows the owner as Florida Assisted Living Affiliation Inc. The property along Miccosukee Road to the east of Kuhlacres Drive is classified as single-family detached. However, the single-family home has been demolished and an assisted living facility is currently under construction. The mixture of existing land uses in the general vicinity is classified as office, medical, and residential. 

 Residential Preservation Analysis 

 The following analysis evaluates whether the subject site is consistent with the characteristics of the Residential Preservation land use category. Policy 2.2.3 [L] sets the following criteria: 

 Existing land use within the area is predominantly residential. 
 Majority of traffic is local in nature. 
 Densities within the area are generally 6 units per acre or less. 
 Existing residential type and density exhibits relatively homogeneous patterns. 
 Assessment of stability of the residential area. 

 The uses to the north of the subject property are predominantly single-family residential. However, existing uses to the east, west, and south are a mixture of office, medical, and a variety of residential types. The uses directly adjacent to Miccosukee Road are predominantly office and medical with some multi-family. While Coombs Drive and Kuhlacres Drive are local roads, Miccosukee Road is a minor arterial roadway with high traffic volume. The subject property is adjacent to residential preservation areas but does not fully meet the criteria for residential preservation. 

 Staff assessed facilities and services and determined that that water, sewer, transportation and schools are available and currently provided to the site. Staff also notes that further assessment of facilities and services, including stormwater, is required during the development review process for specific development projects. 

 Determination for Rezoning 

 The OR-2 zoning district implements the medium density residential office land use pattern of the Suburban future land use map category and the existing office use is an allowed use within the district. The zoning district allows a variety of housing types, compatible non-retail activities of moderate intensity, retail commercial activities (limited to the ground floor of multi-story buildings), and certain community and recreational facilities related to office or residential uses. The maximum height of any potential use is three stories. A list of uses allowed in the OR-2 zoning district can be found in Appendix 2 of the Staff Report (Attachment #2). Sections 10-170 and 10-241 of the Tallahassee Land Development Code, outline the specific provisions of Residential Preservation and Office-Residential – 2, and can be found in Appendix 2 of the Staff Report (Attachment #2). 

 Residential Preservation – 2 (RP-2) (Current) is characterized by existing homogeneous residential areas which are predominantly accessed by local streets. The RP-2 district is intended to preserve low density residential character, protect from incompatible land uses, and prohibit densities in excess of 6 units per acre. Commercial, retail, office, and industrial activities are prohibited in the residential preservation district. 

 Office Residential - 2 (OR-2) (Proposed) is intended to be located within areas designated Suburban on the future land use map where employment and residential uses are encouraged to locate in close proximity to each other. This district is intended to promote urban density and intensity of residential and office uses, and a mixture of permitted uses is promoted to encourage the use of public transit and the efficient use of public infrastructure. Off-street parking facilities in the OR-2 district shall be located and designed to promote convenient access to pedestrian and mass transit facilities. The maximum gross density allowed for new residential development in the OR-2 district is 16 units per acre, while the minimum gross density allowed is 8 units per acre. 

 Additionally, Section 10-177 of the Tallahassee Land Development Code outlines buffering and screening requirements determined by the existing uses that are adjacent to proposed uses. Section 10-429 also describes requirements for buffering and neighborhood compatibility for dense residential uses next to protected residential properties. Applicable development standards may include height step-back requirements or tall tree buffers, restrictions on locations of parking lots, loading zones, equipment, and trash enclosures, no active recreation within 200 feet of single-family residential, additional transparency and façade requirements, and distance requirements for earthwork disturbance. 

 Provided the requested Future Land Use Map amendment is approved, the proposed Office Residential - 2 (OR-2) zoning district implements the Suburban future land use category medium density office residential land use pattern, and conforms to the land development requirements of the OR-2 zoning district. The rezoning would allow the existing office use, unify the zoning designation and remove obsolete LUSPs. 

 Public Comment 
 The Planning Department received three general inquiries for more information about the application. In addition to these three inquiries, comments were received prior to the Local Planning Agency meeting from three residents in opposition to the application. The comments were concerned with the potential for additional traffic that could be generated as a result of increased development at the corner of Miccosukee Road and Kuhlacres Drive. The comments are included in the attached staff report (Attachment #2). 

 Local Planning Agency 
 The Local Planning Agency recommended to find the proposed Future Land Use Map Amendment consistent with the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan, based on the findings and other information contained in the staff report, and to recommend adoption of the proposed amendment. They also voted to find the proposed rezoning consistent with the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan, based on the findings and other information contained in the staff report, and to recommend approval of the proposed rezoning. 

 Summary of Rezoning Recommendations Concurrent with TMA2024 013 
 Local Planning Agency recommendation on proposed concurrent rezoning: Approve . 
 Staff analysis on proposed amendment and concurrent rezoning: Consistent . 

 Options 
 1. Adopt Ordinance No. 24-Z-32, thereby amending the official zoning map from Residential Preservation – 2 (RP-2) to Office Residential – 2 (OR-2) concurrent with the small-scale map amendment TMA2024 013 (1932 Miccosukee Road). 

 2. Do not adopt Ordinance No. 24-Z-32, thereby not amending the official zoning map from Residential Preservation – 2 (RP-2) to Office Residential – 2 (OR-2) concurrent with the small-scale map amendment TMA2024 013 (1932 Miccosukee Road). 

 3. Commission direction. 

 Attachments/References 
 Attachment #1: Ordinance 24-Z-32 
 Attachment #2: Staff Report

 Category 
 14. 6:00 P.M. PUBLIC HEARINGS 
 Subject 
 14.04 First and Only Public Hearing on Ordinance No. 24-Z-35: Amendment of the Official Zoning Map to Change the Zoning Classification from Central Urban – 45 (CU-45) to Central Core (CC) Concurrent with the Small-Scale Map Amendment TMA2024 014 (7.17 acres between W. Virginia St, N Copeland St, W Tennessee St and Dewey Street) -- Artie White, PLACE 
 Type 
 Action, Public Hearing 
 Fiscal Impact 
 No 
 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Adopt Ordinance No. 24-Z-35, thereby amending the official zoning map from Central Urban - 45 (CU-45) to Central Core (CC) concurrent with the small-scale map amendment TMA2024 014. 

 For more information, please contact: Susan Poplin, Administrator at Susan.Poplin@talgov.com or (850) 891-6446 

 Statement of Issue 
 This item provides for the first and only Public Hearing of Ordinance No. 24-Z-35 (Attachment #1) to amend the official zoning map to change the zoning classification from Central Urban - 45 (CU-45) to Central Core (CC) on 7.17 acres NE Corner of Dewey St. and W Tennessee St. between W. Virginia St, N. Copeland St., W. Tennessee St. and Dewey St., concurrent with the small-scale map amendment TMA2024 014 (Dewey Street). 

 This matter is a quasi-judicial proceeding. Any ex parte communications must be disclosed in accordance with the procedure set out in City of Tallahassee Resolution No. 95-R-54. To access Ex Parte Disclosures related to this agenda item, if any, please visit the following web portal: https://clerkpav.talgov.com/exparte/ . 

 For any assistance with accessing or requesting copies of Ex Parte records, please contact the City Treasurer-Clerk’s Office, Records Division at (850) 891-8130 during business hours. 

 An estimate of the direct economic impact of certain proposed ordinances must be disclosed in accordance with Florida Statute 166.041. To access the estimated economic impact related to this agenda item, please visit the following website: https://www.talgov.com/Uploads/Public/Documents/place/comp_plan/2024/tma2024_014_biz.pdf . 

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Adopt Ordinance No. 24-Z-35, thereby amending the official zoning map from Central Urban - 45 (CU-45) to Central Core (CC) concurrent with the small-scale map amendment TMA2024 014. 

 Fiscal Impact 
 None. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 
 This item provides for the first and only public hearing of Ordinance No. 24-Z-35 (Attachment #1) in order to amend the official zoning map to change the zoning classification from Central Urban - 45 (CU-45) to Central Core (CC) for 7.17 acres at the NE corner of Dewey St. and W. Tennessee St. between W. Virginia St, N. Copeland St., W. Tennessee St. and Dewey St. 

 Historic aerial imagery dating back as far 1937 shows that the city block was primarily developed as single-family homes in the 30s, 40s, and 50s. However, the historic zoning was intended for high intensity commercial (C-4) that allowed 48 types of commercial and retail uses including automotive uses with no limitation on intensity, and residential (RM-3) of any type up to 43.6 dwelling units per acre, kindergartens and preschools, churches and schools, and studios. Other related restricted uses included commercial convenience and services, fraternities and sororities, and universities. 

 Following a nation-wide trend, many structures appear to have redeveloped in a suburban and parkway development style featuring drive-thru restaurants and businesses fronting arterial roadways through the 60s, 70s, and 80s. 

 Since the 80s, the block’s development pattern has remained largely unchanged while redevelopment has grown out to meet the city block from all sides, primarily spurred by Tallahassee’s downtown and Florida State University. 

 A limited use site plan (LUSP) was established on one of the subject parcels at the corner of N Copeland Street and W Virginia Street in 1986. The LUSP was adopted by Ordinance 86-O-2572. The LUSP is obsolete and may create confusion in the application of development standards. The proposed rezoning will address the LUSP as part of the proposed amendment to the Official Zoning Map. If the proposed rezoning is approved, the LUSP will be repealed. 

 The LUSP established commercial at the corner, specifically C-1 commercial uses which include a variety of commercial such as banks, restaurants and daycare centers, retail uses such as drug stores, bakeries, food and groceries, and any type of residential up to 18 dwelling units per acre. The previous zoning was RM-3 which allowed residential any type up to 43.6 dwelling units, kindergartens and preschools, churches and schools, and studios. Other related restricted uses included commercial convenience and services, fraternities and sororities, and universities. 

 The effect of the rezoning (accompanying the proposed land use change TMA2024 014) would be to recognize the establish Central Core land use and zoning for this urban area within the Downtown overlay and to remove the obsolete LUSP. Details of the proposed change are found in the attached Staff Report (Attachment #2). 

 Adjacent and Existing Uses and Site Plan Analysis 

 The proposed Central Core land use district and zoning is compatible with adjacent land uses. The proposed land use district is intended to complement a high-activity 18-hour downtown, of which it is directly adjacent to the south and east. Additionally, the proposed land use district has the ability to complement Florida State University directly to the south and west, allowing for high density residential and multi-use buildings that promote pedestrian, bicycle, and transit use. 

 Staff assessed facilities and services and determined that water, sewer, transportation and schools are available and currently provided to the site. The Leon County School District approved a School Impact Analysis indicating that additional coordination is required when a project is proposed. Staff notes that further assessment of facilities and services, including schools and stormwater, is required during the development review process for specific development projects. 

 Greater Frenchtown/Southside CRA 
 The amendment area is located within both the Frenchtown Neighborhood Boundary as well as the Frenchtown/Southside Community Redevelopment Area (CRA). The 2021 Greater Frenchtown Southside Redevelopment Plan identifies Tennessee Street as a corridor with redevelopment opportunities. This plan also identifies parking as an issue associated with higher intensity development impacting roadways north of Tennessee Street. The plan identifies student housing as an encroaching threat on the character of the Frenchtown Neighborhood. 
 Frenchtown Neighborhood First Plan 
 The Frenchtown Neighborhood First Plan (Plan) was presented in 2020. The Plan identified the neighborhood boundary as being generally between Tennessee Street to the south, Woodward Avenue to the west, 7th Avenue to the north and Adams Street to the east. 

 In analyzing the details of the Neighborhood First Plan, staff notes the proposed amendment does not create inconsistencies with the existing Plan. The Plan acknowledges high intensity areas, including W Tennessee Street, and prescribes limitations or prohibitions of expansions into the low-density residential areas of the neighborhood. The subject block is not proposing extension into low-density areas of the neighborhood and is not abutting or adjacent to low-density areas, including Residential Preservation areas. Additionally, the plan discusses the neighborhood and preventing displacement of residents from student housing. The amendment will avoid displacement of residents due to the fact that the block is primarily non-residential development. 
 Regardless of the Plan, the current land use and zoning allow high density residential development which would allow a variety of housing types. Staff also notes that the “gateway” planning area does not include the subject block because it is focused and prescribed for Macomb Street. The proposed amendment would not affect either of the above Plan provisions, and would not preclude any of the Plan prescriptions for future coordination and review of proposed development and redevelopment projects in the Frenchtown Neighborhood area. Additional analysis details as well as related public comments are found in the Staff Report, Attachment #2. 

 Determination for Rezoning 

 The proposed Central Core zoning district is intended to be located in areas designated as Central Core on the Future Land Use Map of the Tallahassee-Leon County Comprehensive Plan. The zoning district descriptions below provide information about intent and allowed uses. Sections 239.4 and 10-197 of the Land Development Code, outline the specific provisions of the Central Urban – 45 (CU-45) and the Central Core (CC) zoning districts, and can be found in Appendix 2 of the attached Staff Report (Attachment #2). 

 Central Urban - 45 (CU-45) (Current) is intended to promote infill and redevelopment of urban areas with sufficient supporting infrastructure, accessibility to services, and proximity to the Downtown and universities. The district provides for medium and high density residential, office and commercial district. CU-45 provides for up to 45 dwelling units per acre and 200,000 sf of nonresidential per parcel. 

 Central Core (CC) (Proposed) is intended to promote infill and redevelopment of existing residential urban areas with sufficient supporting infrastructure, accessibility to services, and proximity to the Capital, employment centers, and universities, promote compatibility between adjacent residential and non-residential uses through high quality design, and promote pedestrian and bicycle mobility. The CC zoning district allows residential density up to 150 dwelling units per acre. 

 Expanding the Central Core land use requires that it be within the Downtown overlay and that it meet three criteria. The entirety of the subject area is within the Downtown Overlay and the criteria are analyzed below. 

 1) Is the site contiguous with the existing Central Core land use district? 
 Yes, the applicant’s “Subject Site” as well as the Planning Department’s “Expansion Area” are contiguous with the Central Core land use district to the south and east. 

 2) Does the site have the available infrastructure? 
 Yes, the subject site is located within the urban services area and has direct access to state and local roads, as well as available sewer and water services. 

 3) Does the proposed parcel exhibit a need for the development? 
 There is no specific development plan accompanying the proposed amendment. Staff notes that acquisition and aggregation of parcels in the existing Central Core land use district is logistically and financially difficult to facilitate quality development and redevelopment. There appears to be a lack of sizable parcels within the existing Central Core district. A 2023 analysis of the Central Core district found that while there were several vacant parcels present, there were only three parcels of the same approximate size (or larger) to the Subject Site (~ 2 acres). Of these three sites, one has been developed, while the other two are used as parking. Future redevelopment could catalyze other improvements on Tennessee Street and promote infill development. 

 Provided the requested Future Land Use Map amendment is approved, the proposed Central Core zoning district implements the Central Core land use category and conforms to the land development requirements of the CC zoning district. The subject properties are located contiguous to the Central Core zoning district, are within the Downtown Overlay District, and have sufficient supporting infrastructure with proximity to the Capital, employment centers, and universities. 

 Summary of Rezoning Concurrent with TMA2024 014 
 Local Planning Agency recommendation on proposed concurrent rezoning: Approve (6-0) . 
 Staff analysis on proposed amendment and concurrent rezoning: Consistent . 

 Options 
 1. Adopt Ordinance No. 24-Z-35, thereby amending the official zoning map from Central Urban - 45 (CU-45) to Central Core (CC) concurrent with the small-scale map amendment TMA2024 014. 

 2. Do not adopt Ordinance No. 24-Z-35, thereby not amending the official zoning map from Central Urban - 45 (CU-45) to Central Core (CC) concurrent with the small-scale map amendment TMA2024 014. 

 3. Commission direction.

 Attachment #2: Staff Report

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Approve the Purchase Order Authorization for Hopkins Unit 2A Refurbished Gas Turbine Rotor Purchase from General Electric. 

 For more information, please contact: Tony Guillen, General Manager- Electric & Gas Utility, 850-891-5534 or Eric Walters, Assistant General Manager - Energy Supply, 850-891-5034 

 Statement of Issue 
 Hopkins Unit 2A (HP2A) was placed in commercial operation in 2008. The combustion turbine was manufactured by General Electric (GE). GE has established that the combustion turbine rotor has an estimated useful life of 144,000 service hours. Any operations beyond the established end-of-life hours would not be supported by GE or the Long-Term Service Agreement (LTSA) contract between GE and the City. By spring of 2027, the rotor is expected to reach its expected end of life. 

 This agenda item requests approval to purchase a replacement rotor from General Electric for the 2027 installation.  Funding for a replacement combustion turbine rotor is currently budgeted for FY2025. 

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Approve the Purchase Order Authorization for Hopkins Unit 2A Refurbished Gas Turbine Rotor Purchase from General Electric. 

 Fiscal Impact 
 Estimated at $8,650,000. Funding will be provided from the approved capital budget. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 
 Hopkins Station Unit 2/2A is a 300MW Combined Cycle unit and stands as the largest and most efficient unit in the City’s energy generation fleet. The unit includes a GE Gas Turbine, a Nooter Erikson Heat Recovery Steam Generator, and a Westinghouse Steam Turbine. Since its commissioning in 2008, HP2A has accrued over 125,000 hours of operation. 

 By 2027, it will reach the rotor’s end of life at 144,000 operating hours, which coincides with its scheduled Major Inspection outage. The rotor is removed during the Major Inspection outage as part of that planned maintenance. A new or refurbished rotor will either need to be on hand for replacement or sent out for refurbishment.  

 Energy Supply Staff evaluated multiple options and considered economic impacts, operational risks, and potential reliability or efficiency improvements. The options included: 

 Refurbished rotor purchase (recommended option) – $8,650,000
Considered the best economic value based on cost and net present value. This option offers robust reliability improvements, similar to a new rotor, without increasing the outage duration. However, it does not include guaranteed output or efficiency improvements. 

 New rotor purchase – $14,450,000
While this option provides strong reliability and avoids added outage time, it is less economical than the refurbished rotor and does not include guaranteed performance improvements. 

 Rotor Life Extension (RLE) of existing rotor – $6,000,000
This lower-cost option would require a minimum of six months of downtime, with the potential for additional delays and cost increases depending on the rotor’s condition once disassembled and inspected. 

 Non-OEM new rotor purchase – $15,000,000
The most expensive and least favorable option. In addition to its higher cost, it would negate Rotor, Compressor, and Casing coverage under the existing Long-Term Service Agreement (LTSA) with GE. 

 Funding will be provided from the approved capital budg et. 

 Department(s) Review 
 Procurement, Resource Management 

 Options 
 1. Approve the Purchase Order Authorization for Hopkins Unit 2A Refurbished Gas Turbine Rotor Purchase from General Electric. 
 Pros: Purchasing a refurbished rotor will provide a significant cost savings for the City. 

 Cons: A refurbished rotor typically has a lifespan of approximately 12 years. 

 2. Do not approve the Purchase Order Authorization for the Hopkins Unit 2A Refurbished Gas Turbine Rotor Purchase from General Electric and provide Commission direction. 
 Pros: Investing in a new rotor will significantly enhance its longevity, with an expected lifespan of around 18 years. 

 Cons: The price of purchasing a new rotor is significantly greater than the cost of acquiring a refurbished rotor. 

 Attachments/References 
 None

 For more information, please contact: Tony Guillen, General Manager - Electric & Gas Utility, 850-891-5534, or Greg Ozbun, Assistant General Manager - System Operations, 850-891-3030 

 Statement of Issue 
 The Outage Management System (OMS) is the hardware and software platform the Electric & Gas Utility (E&G) uses to monitor electric outages and ensure system reliability. This system is essential for managing customer outage notifications and supporting efficient restoration efforts. The current OMS was purchased in 2015 through the Smart Grid Improvement Grant and is approaching end of life, with vendor technical support scheduled to end January 1, 2027. E&G is transitioning to a Software as a Service (SaaS) and managed services model to ensure continued service reliability and access to technical support. 

 In collaboration with Technology & Innovation (T&I) and Customer Operations, E&G staff developed the statement of work and technical specifications for a replacement system. Procurement Services issued a Request for Proposals (RFP-035-25-CW) for the new OMS and received six proposals. Following a thorough evaluation process, the review committee recommends TRC Engineers, Inc. as the most responsive and qualified vendor. 

 This agenda item seeks City Commission approval to award the contract for the replacement Outage Management System to TRC Engineers, Inc., and to authorize the City Manager or his designee to negotiate and execute the contract. 

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Approve the award of RFP-035-25-CW for the Replacement Outage Management System to TRC Engineers, Inc., and authorize the City Manager or his designee to negotiate and execute a contract. 

 Fiscal Impact 
 The estimated total fiscal impact of the contract is $5,109,441. Funding for the first year, totaling $1,850,000, is available in the approved capital budget. Funding for years two through six will be provided through the City’s approved operating or capital budgets. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 
 The Electric & Gas Utility (E&G) originally acquired the current Outage Management System (OMS) through a Smart Grid Improvement Grant as a single-source purchase, utilizing a master services agreement with Technology & Innovation (T&I). This approach ensured continued compatibility with the City’s Geographic Information System (GIS), allowing for more precise GIS map integration while reducing the required staff time. Additionally, the OMS was integrated with the Honeywell Advanced Meter Infrastructure (AMI) system to receive automated outage notifications, improving response efficiency. 

 Schneider Electric, the current OMS vendor, notified the City that support for the existing OMS platform will end on January 1, 2027. After that date, the vendor will no longer provide technical support, even during outage events. Given the critical role the OMS plays in electric service restoration efforts, planning was initiated to procure a replacement system through a competitive solicitation process. 

 A cross-departmental evaluation committee was assembled, including representatives from T&I, Customer Operations, E&G Power Delivery, and E&G System Operations. Procurement Services issued RFP-035-25-CW for replacing the OMS. 47 vendors downloaded the solicitation, with six submitting formal proposals. After reviewing the submissions, the committee shortlisted two firms: CGI Technologies and Solutions, Inc., and TRC Engineers, Inc. (also known as TRC Solutions). Following vendor presentations, the committee unanimously recommended awarding the contract to TRC Engineers, Inc. 

 The new OMS will introduce several enhanced features not currently available in the existing system. These improvements will expand dispatching capabilities during electric outages and enhance customers' overall system reliability. Moreover, the updated platform will position the City to more easily incorporate future upgrades to the AMI system and other operational enhancements. 

 The approved capital budget will fund the first year of the contract, which includes implementation, annual licensing, cloud hosting, and managed services. The current available balance for this project is $1,850,000. Funding for subsequent years (years two through six) will come from the City’s approved operating or capital budgets.

Agenda Item Details 

 Meeting 
 May 14, 2025 - City Commission Meeting & Summary 
 Category 
 11. INTRODUCTION OF ORDINANCES 
 Subject 
 11.03 Introduction of Ordinance 25-O-13, Amending Chapter 7 of the Code of Ordinances, the Tallahassee Municipal Election Code; Set the First and Only Public Hearing for June 11, 2025 at 6pm at City Hall -- James O. Cooke, IV, City Treasurer-Clerk 
 Type 
 Action, Introduction of Ordinance 
 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Introduce Ordinance 25-O-13, Amending Chapter 7 of the Code of Ordinances, the Tallahassee Municipal Election Code; Set the first and only public hearing for June 11, 2025 at 6pm at City Hall. 

 For more information, please contact Matt Lutz, Records Administrator at (850) 891-8130. 

 Statement of Issue 
 Chapter 7 of the Code of General Ordinances comprises the election code governing municipal elections of the City of Tallahassee. The last significant amendments to this chapter occurred in 2004. In the past twenty years, much has changed in the Florida Elections Code (Chapters 97-106, F.S.). In addition, a City Charter amendment was passed at the 2024 general election, changing how municipal primary elections are conducted. For these reasons, staff have performed a thorough review of the city’s election code and have drafted a proposed ordinance to modernize the city’s procedures and to enact the voter-approved changes for primary elections. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 
 Since at least 1957, the city’s local election code has stated municipal elections are conducted in substantial conformance with the processes and procedures set forth in the Florida Election Code, unless the city code provides otherwise. Per §100.3605, F.S., municipalities are afforded autonomy to promulgate their own election procedures, so long as those procedures are not contrary to any component of the Florida Election Code that expressly applies to municipalities. If the local election code does not address a certain aspect of conducting an election, then state law specifies that the Florida Election Code provisions control. 

 Since a successful March 2004 ballot initiative amended the city charter, the city’s primary and regular elections for electing members to the city commission have been held in conjunction with county elections. The city election code was amended in Spring 2004 to enact this referendum’s requirements. Since that time, city elections have coincided with state & federal elections and the county canvassing board has been responsible for tabulating and certifying the official election results. The city has conducted only one standalone city election since 2004, which was a November 2005 straw poll. This was a mail-ballot-only election and was conducted at sole city expense of $337,256. As a mail-only election, the election results were certified by the county canvassing board, as required by the Florida Election Code. The city commission, sitting as a city canvassing board, has not convened since February 2003. As such, there has not been occasion prompting a review of the city’s election code, as codified in Chapter 7 of the code book. 

 With passage of the November 2024 charter amendment governing the conduct of municipal primary elections, staff commenced a full review of the municipal election code and reviewed the election codes of peer cities. Additionally, staff reviewed the election records of city races dating back to 2004, examining turnout, amounts raised by candidates, those qualifying via petitions or as write-in candidates, etc. With insights gleaned from this work, staff have drafted a modernized Tallahassee Municipal Election Code, as summarized below. This draft was reviewed by the Leon County Supervisor of Elections, and adjustments have been made based on feedback received by the Supervisor’s staff. The draft was subsequently reviewed by the City Attorney’s Office and is summarized below. 

 Summary of Proposed Tallahassee Municipal Election Code 

 Article I 

 Sec. 7-1 – Provides a Title for this chapter of the City Code. 

 Sec. 7-2 – Provides that the Florida Election Code will control, unless the city code provides a procedure unique to Tallahassee. (see §100.3605, F.S.) 

 Sec. 7-3 – Specifies Tallahassee elections are non-partisan. While city elections conducted since 1921 have been conducted on a non-partisan basis, this fact has never been formally codified in the city code. 

 Sec. 7-4 – Recognizes Ch. 97, F.S., and more specifically §97.105, F.S. which implements a permanent single voter registration system for Florida, and §166.032, F.S. concerning municipal electors. 

 Article II 

 Sec. 7-21 – Defines eligibility criteria for those seeking election or appointment to municipal office. Registered electors who have resided in the city limits for at least one year are eligible. For purposes of determining a candidate’s eligibility, the voter registration records will control. 

 Sec. 7-22 – Implements §120 of the City Charter with respect to dates of the candidate qualifying period. 

 Sec. 7-23 – Provides for three distinct ways a person can qualify as a candidate for city commission: 1) by payment of a filing fee, 2) by collecting signatures on a candidate petition, or 3) as a write-in candidate. There is a mandatory state election assessment that must be paid, except by write-in candidates (see Fla. Division of Elections opinion, DE 97-02). 

 Sec. 7-24 – Provides for how vacancies in candidacy will be handled, should one or more candidates in a particular contest withdraw, die, or are removed by court action. Such procedures are mandated by §166.031(6). 

 Article III 

 Sec. 7-41 – Specifies the City Treasurer-Clerk is the chief elections official for the City. Since 1984, the City has contracted with the Supervisor for the conduct of municipal elections. Should the city commission conduct a standalone city election, subsection (c) requires the commission, by resolution, to establish procedures for any such election. With this language, City Commission Policy 118, concerning canvassing of absentee ballots, can be repealed as obsolete. 

 Sec. 7-42 - Implements §120 of the City Charter with respect to dates of the general election and the primary election, if a primary is required per this Code. 

 Sec. 7-43 – Implements the 2024 charter amendment with respect to 2-regular-candidate races. A primary is only required for contests wherein three or more candidates have qualified, none of whom are write-in candidates. As required by §101.151(2)b, write-in candidates compete only in a general election. The section also governs ascertaining the results of a primary election. 

 Sec. 7-44 – Details who appears on a general election ballot and governs ascertaining the results of a general election. 

 Sec. 7-45 – Specifies the precincts that will be utilized, should the city conduct a standalone city election. 

 Sec. 7-46 – Specifies the city commission will establish the polling places, and provide public notice thereof, should the city conduct a standalone election. 

 Article IV 

 Sec. 7-61 – Implements §123 of the City Charter with respect to canvassing the results of an election held concurrent with a state or federal election. 

 Sec. 7-62 – Implements §123 of the City Charter with respect to canvassing the results of an election not held concurrent with a state or federal election. 

 Sec. 7-63 – Provides that all commissioners, the mayor, and the four appointed officials will be administered a formal oath of office during an open, noticed public meeting. 

 Article V 

 Sec. 7-81 – Implements the provisions of §166.031, F.S. with respect to a city charter amendments referendum initiated by submission of a petition signed by at least 10% of registered voters. This section is being relocated from §2-2 of the City Code as the subject matter is more closely aligned with Elections. 

 The proposed ordinance corrects a conflict between the existing Chapter 7 language and state law concerning the mandatory 1% election assessment that is collected and remitted to the State (s. 99.093, F.S.). In comparison with the current Chapter 7 language, these amendments will reinstate a city filing fee for candidates seeking to qualify to run for city office. In addition to the mandatory 1% state assessment, Florida municipalities may implement a local filing fee. In review of other Florida municipalities, there are a wide variety of local filing fee models, some based on a percentage of salary ranging from 1% to 5%, others a fixed dollar amount, and others who have no fee, but usually require petitions be gathered. The proposed 3% filing fee is consistent with the 3% filing fee currently in place for all non-partisan Leon County positions, including candidates for judge, school board, and county commission. 

 As proposed, the ordinance also remedies a conflict between the existing language of Ch. 7, §120 of the Charter, and state law with regards to the number of required petitions that must be gathered by persons choosing that means of qualifying. State law requires those qualifying via petitions to collect petitions equal to 1% of the number of registered voters in the preceding general election. There were nearly 122,000 voters registered in the 2024 municipal general election. 2003 was the last known time a city candidate qualified by the petition method. 

 In addition, language has been proposed to have appointed officials formally sworn in at the start of their service. This is common in many other cities. Given that City of Tallahassee elected officials, police officers, and firefighters are formally sworn in, staff suggests that appointed officials also be sworn in during an open meeting. 

 Options 
 1. Introduce Ordinance 25-O-13, Amending Chapter 7 of the Code of Ordinances, the Tallahassee Municipal Election Code; Set the first and only public hearing for June 11, 2025, at 6pm at City Hall. 

 2. Provide other direction. 

 Attachments 
 Attachment 1 – Ordinance 25-O-13 
 Attachment 2 – Current Chapter 7 of the City Code

Agenda Item Details

 Category 
 8. CONSENT 
 Subject 
 8.03 Approval for Procurement of Meter Testing Equipment – Automated Platform Meter Testing Equipment & Portable Meter Analyzing Equipment -- Tony Guillen, Electric & Gas Utility 
 Type

 Dollar Amount

 Budget Source

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Approve a single-source purchase from Radian Research Inc. and issue a purchase order for approximately $360,850 for testing equipment, including four WECO 4050 test platforms and two RW-31 portable analyzers with associated accessories. 

 For more information, please contact: Tony Guillen, General Manager- Electric & Gas Utility, 850-891-5534 or Greg Ozbun, Assistant General Manager - System, 850-891-3030 

 Statement of Issue 
 The Electric & Gas Utility’s current desktop and portable electric meter testing equipment has reached the end of its serviceable life and is no longer supported with replacement parts. The desktop units, Radian Research WECO 2350 platforms, were purchased over a decade ago and are now failing to meet national calibration standards required for accurate energy measurement. These standards are critical to ensure the integrity of meter testing, which directly impacts billing accuracy and system reliability. The aging equipment limits the Utility’s ability to test and verify new meters and redeploy existing ones efficiently. 

 Similarly, the Utility’s portable field analyzers, including the RM-17 and RB-20 units, are no longer adequate for modern testing needs. These devices lack capabilities such as reverse current testing (needed for solar customers), automated data recording, and complete three-phase analysis. In addition, they have shown issues with false test indications and unreliable documentation, undermining field testing operations. 

 This item seeks approval to purchase updated desktop and portable testing equipment from Radian Research Inc. to replace the obsolete systems, restore full compliance with national standards, and enhance operational accuracy in both laboratory and field settings. 

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1: Approve a single-source purchase from Radian Research Inc. and issue a purchase order for approximately $360,850 for testing equipment, including four WECO 4050 test platforms and two RW-31 portable analyzers with associated accessories. 

 Fiscal Impact 
 The total investment of approximately $360,850 will be funded through the approved capital budget. This procurement will ensure the continued accuracy and efficiency of electric meter testing, both in the lab and in the field. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 

 History/Facts & Issues 

 The Electric & Gas Utility is seeking approval to purchase updated electric meter testing equipment from Radian Research Inc. to replace obsolete desktop and portable systems that have reached the end of their serviceable life. The current desktop units, Radian Research WECO 2350 platforms, were purchased over a decade ago and are no longer supported with replacement parts. These units now frequently fail to meet national calibration standards, which are critical for ensuring the accuracy of energy measurements and the reliability of customer billing. As a result, the Utility’s ability to test and verify new meters, as well as to redeploy existing ones, has become increasingly limited and inefficient. 

 To address these issues, the Utility proposes acquiring new Radian Research WECO 4050 automated test platforms. These updated systems will restore compliance with national calibration requirements and significantly improve the efficiency and reliability of the meter testing and deployment process. 

 In addition, the Utility’s current portable field analyzers—specifically the RM-17 for single-phase meters and the RB-20 for three-phase meters, are no longer adequate for modern field operations. The RM-17 cannot test reverse current flow, which is essential for customers with solar photovoltaic systems, and lacks automated data recording. The RB-20, while capable of handling three-phase meters, can only test one phase at a time, limiting field efficiency. Both devices have also shown issues with false test results and unreliable documentation, posing operational risks. 

 To modernize field testing capabilities, the Utility seeks to purchase Radian Research RW-31 portable analyzers. These will become the primary tools for three-phase testing and allow the RB-20 units to be reassigned to single-phase testing, effectively replacing the RM-17 devices. This upgrade will ensure more accurate, reliable, and efficient field testing, supporting both customer service and operational performance. 

 Overall, this investment will enhance the Utility’s ability to maintain accurate metering, support renewable energy customers, comply with regulatory standards, and deliver high-quality service to its more than 125,000 electric customers. 

 Department(s) Review 
 Procurement Services, Resource Management 

 Options 
 1. Approve a single-source purchase from Radian Research Inc. and issue a purchase order for approximately $360,850 for testing equipment, including four WECO 4050 test platforms and two RW-31 portable analyzers with associated accessories. 

 Pros: 
 Improved customer service through more accurate and reliable lab and field meter testing data. 
 The new WECO 4050 automated test platforms will resolve calibration issues, meet national reference standards, and enhance efficiency in testing new meters. 
 The new WECO RW-31 portable analyzers will serve as the primary testing equipment for three-phase meters, allowing the RB-20 units to be repurposed for single-phase-testing and enabling the retirement of outdated RM-17 units. 

 Cons: Ongoing annual calibration and maintenance will be required to ensure continued accuracy and extend the equipment’s service life. 

 2. Reject the procurement request of the Radian Research three-phase automated test platforms WECO 4050 and Radian Research three-phase portable analyzers WECO RW-31 and provide Commission direction. 

 Pros: Funds currently allocated for this purchase could be redirected to support other Electric & Gas Utility priorities, if the equipment is not procured. 

 Cons: 
 The City and its customers will to face inefficiencies in meter testing and deployment. 
 Operational risks will persist due to reliance on outdated and unsupported equipment.

 Attachment 1 - Radian Research Quote for WECO 4050 automated test platforms, reference standard, optical ports, and adapter kit 
 Attachment 2 - Radian Research Quote for WECO RW-31 portable analyzers, optical ports, and cable kits

 Statement of Issue 
 Routine firefighter physical examinations are key to reducing job related injuries and ensuring our public safety officials remain fit for service.  Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 
 History/Facts & Issues 
 The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) is a trusted industry source on fire and life safety issues. NFPA promulgates codes and standards to help protect people, property, businesses, and communities and establishes minimum safety requirements. NFPA Standard 1582 provides an occupational medical program to reduce risks and provide for the health and safety of firefighters. NFPA Standard 1583 provides a complete health-related fitness program (HRFP) for firefighters. 
 Reducing firefighter job related risk is of prime importance to the City of Tallahassee and the Tallahassee Fire Department. Life Extension Clinics, Inc., d/b/a LifeScan Wellness Centers, will conduct comprehensive and efficient firefighter physical examination with stress testing on location. By delivering services on-site, the Fire Department can reduce downtime and curb overtime costs. 
 Life Extension Clinics, Inc. d/b/a LifeScan Wellness Centers uses an integrated medical approach compliant with NFPA 1582 and 1583 specifically designed for public safety personnel to support early detection of health issues and ensure fitness for duty. The medical reviews will include ultrasounds, cancer screening, and cardiovascular scans for improved diagnoses and best outcomes for firefighters.

If approved, this proposed single source procurement contract is a two-year award with options for two one-year extensions.

 As requested by the City Commission, this item provides an update on the City of Tallahassee’s E-Scooter Shared Micromobility Program (Program). 

 Recommended Action 
 Option 1 - Accept the status update on the City of Tallahassee Micromobility Program. 

 Fiscal Impact 
 This item does not have a fiscal impact to the City. However, if the Program is discontinued, there will be a loss of revenue to the City. The program generated $60,883.60 for the General Fund in 2025 and has generated over $650,000 since the inception of the pilot and the permanent program. 

 Supplemental Material/Issue Analysis 
 History/Facts & Issues 
 Since 2019, the City of Tallahassee has sought to provide micromobility services through one or more e-scooter vendors. The City’s initial efforts included research on existing programs elsewhere in the Country, identification of requirements for facilities and infrastructure, a review of statutory regulations and policy framework, local ordinance development including legal issues and liabilities, and vendor contract development to operate and manage the program. At the time, the micro-mobility industry and motorized scooter technology was relatively new and rapidly evolving. Other programs were experiencing varying levels of success with motorized scooters. 

 After considering the various information provided by staff, the City Commission directed staff on May 15, 2019, to issue a Request for Information (RFI) to obtain information from interested e-scooter companies for a pilot program, including recommended pilot parameters presented by staff. 

 On June 19, 2019, the Commission directed staff to invite five e-scooters vendors, including the current vendor Spin, to apply for a permit to be a part of a three-month pilot program. Due to successful operation of the pilot program and the intent to provide vendors adequate time to establish a market, the City Commission directed staff on September 25, 2019, to extend the pilot program. 

 On January 29, 2020, the Commission directed staff to bring back an ordinance to adopt a permanent micromobility program. Under Florida Law, e-scooters are granted all the rights and duties of bicycles. By having an ordinance regulating shared micromobility devices, the City controls how e-scootershare vendors may operate within the City limits. If the City does not have a micromobility ordinance in place (regulating e-scootershare companies), then an unlimited number of vendors could operate freely, without the strict limitations on where e-scooters can be deployed, operated, or end their ride, except as otherwise provided by Florida Law. At the January 29, 2020, meeting, the Commission also directed staff to release a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) to procure vendors to participate in a shared micromobility program and to extend the pilot program while the permanent program was being established. 

 On September 9, 2020, the City Commission approved the RFQ evaluation committee’s ranking and authorized the City manager to execute operating agreements with two vendors, Spin and Veo. An Operating Agreement was entered into with Spin on October 15, 2020 (See Attachment #2). An Operating Agreement was also entered into with Veo, but Veo subsequently left the Tallahassee market. In April 2024, Spin was purchased by a new company, Blue Jay Transit, Inc., doing business as Pheenix USH LLC and the City was provided necessary updated insurance and licensure documents. The Operating Agreement with Spin is up for renewal. 

 Summary of the E-Scooter Program 
 Since October 15, 2020, the City has permitted micro-mobility services, or e-scooters as they are commonly known, via the Program. Since inception, the program has seen 663,870 rides by residents and visitors covering over 822,000 miles and brought in over $650,000.00 in revenue. These trips offset 42 metric tons of carbon, according to an emissions calculator housed by the Environmental Protection Agency. This is the equivalent to 46,654 pounds of coal burned, or the amount of energy it takes to power nearly 3.4 million smartphones. Attachment #3 provides a summary of stats from the Program. Additionally, the Program’s sole vendor, Spin, has provided services for various events such as DJ Demp week, and for a number of organization tours such as Youth Leadership Tallahassee, and other various e-bike exploration events. 

 Table 1. Number of Rides by Micromobility Devices by Year

 Table 1 shows the number of rides by year. As shown in Table 1, rides have decreased since 2023. The likely reasons for this decreased ridership are the proliferation of privately-owned scooters and the establishment of no-ride zones at Cascades Park and other public spaces where e-scooters were being utilized for recreational purposes. This has resulted in a situation where those utilizing e-scooters in the Program are likely doing so to meet transportation needs instead of recreational purposes. 

 General Program Requirements: 
 Below is a listing of the general program requirements that approved vendors are required to abide by: 

 The Micro-Mobility program runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week. 
 E-scooters must be rebalanced each day to set locations. 
 E-scooters must not block access, including ADA access, sidewalks, and doorways. 
 The vendor must have local, on-the-ground support. 
 The vendor must provide all required data on number of rides, deployments, etc. 
 The vendor must provide safety information and should provide helmet programs and participate in safety events. 
 The vendor must provide a hurricane safety plan. 
 FSU/FAMU/TSC are no-ride zones for e-scooters unless the education facility chooses to participate in the program. 
 Cascades Park, the Florida State Capitol, and other specifically designated areas are no-ride zones for scooters and blocked with geofencing. The City may require the vendor to geofence any areas at its sole discretion. 
 E-scooters are limited to operating at 14 mph. 

 E-Scooter Interactions with Tallahassee Police Department 
 Staff from the Tallahassee Police Department conduct a monthly review of police reports that include interactions with Program e-scooters. This allows program staff to track collisions, traffic infractions, and criminality. These tracking activities started during the pilot in 2019 and are ongoing. Since 2019, TPD has logged 145 police interactions with e-scooters. The majority of these interactions are traffic law enforcement and responding to accidents. Attachment #4 provides information on all 145 interactions. 
 In 2024 and 2025 there were 16 total incidents logged by TPD. Of these 16 reports, eight (8) were traffic collision related. 
 There has not been a reported incident with an e-scooter within the micromobility program since May 2025. 

 Community Input 
Dr. Erwin Jackson spoke at the November 19, 2025, City Commission Meeting regarding issues with e-scooters and properties he owns. Staff met with Dr. Jackson in preparation of this status update. Dr. Jackson owns numerous residential properties in Tallahassee including two on Jackson Bluff Road and one on Nylic Street, which are close to FSU's Campus. At the outset of the Program, employees of Dr. Jackson would collect any scooters left on his properties by users and hold them in his office, where e-scooter vendors, including Spin, would collect them during rebalancing. 

 According to documents provided by Dr. Jackson (Attachment #6), beginning in June 2021, Dr. Jackson began holding scooters, including Spin's, and presenting bills to the vendors for storing the scooters when they came to collect the e-scooters. To date, no vendors have paid Dr. Jackson or Jackson Properties. In 2024, Spin geofenced off three of Dr. Jackson's properties on Jackson Bluff Road and Nylic Street. Documents provided by Dr. Jackson indicate that he has 49 Spin scooters in storage. Dr. Jackson argues that the City is owed $11,379,800 (based on his calculation, using the storage fee provided in the operating agreement for when the City collects an e-scooter after a vendor has failed to comply with direction from the City to address an issue with an e-scooter) and that he is owed $1,137,980 by Spin (again, based on his calculation, using a $20 per scooter, per day fee) for storing these scooters. 

 Spin provided a letter summarizing recent communications with Dr. Jackson (Attachment #7). In this letter they contend that Jackson Properties does not have the authority to take or hold their e-scooters, nor charge a fee for their release, because they are not a licensed tow business. Spin believes Jackson Properties is unlawfully holding their property. 

 Staff does not believe the City can impose any penalties or fines for the scooters Dr. Jackson indicates are in his possession. This unresolved issue is between Dr. Jackson and Spin. 

 Other Relevant Information 
 This section provides other information relevant regarding micromobility and the City’s micromobility City of Tallahassee’s E-Scooter Shared Micromobility Program. 

 E-Scooter Ordinance 
 Under Section 316.2128(1), Florida Statutes, the operator of a motorized scooter or micromobility device has all of the rights and duties applicable to the rider of a bicycle under applicable Florida law. However, this section indicates that local governments may adopt an ordinance governing the operation of micromobility devices and motorized scooters on streets, highways, sidewalks, and sidewalk areas under the local government’s jurisdiction. The City of Tallahassee’s e-scooter ordinance outlines clear parameters for how an e-scooter company may operate within City limits, such as requirements for responses due to ADA issues, or requirements to create no-ride zones. Should the City Commission repeal the micromobility (Ordinance No. 2020-O-09AA), nothing would prevent, or limit, e-scooter companies from entering the market and operating without restriction, except as provided by general Florida law. 

 Operating Agreement with Spin 
 The operating agreement with Spin, the sole e-scooter vendor operating in the Tallahassee market, is currently month to month and due to be renewed. Unless alternative direction is provided by the City Commission, the renewal of this operating agreement is within the authority of the City Manager. Not renewing the operating agreement would revoke Spin’s authorization to operate within the City’s jurisdiction. This would effectively end the e-scooter program until such a time as the City Commission directs staff to reissue a RFQ as provided below. 

 Conclusion 
 The City of Tallahassee has managed a micromobility program since 2019 to support the community’s multi-modal approach to transportation. Since inception, the program has seen 663,870 rides by residents and visitors covering over 822,000 miles. 

 This item provides a brief history of the City of Tallahassee’s E-Scooter Shared Micromobility Program, information on the current parameters and operations of the Program, and other relevant information regarding the Program.

 1. Accept the status update on the City of Tallahassee Shared Micromobility Program. 

 2. Commission direction.
